Created
kree-AY-ted
v. (past part.)
From Latin creare, to bring forth, to produce, to make. Webster 1828: formed from nothing; caused to exist. The Hebrew bara that stands behind the word in Genesis is used in the Old Testament only with God as its subject — no creature ever bara.

Biblical Definition

Created is the fourth word of the Bible and it settles everything that follows: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth (Genesis 1:1). There is no pre-existing material, no rival, no struggle, and no process; there is God, and then there is a universe because He spoke. The Hebrew verb bara takes only God as its subject throughout the Old Testament, which is Scripture’s own way of marking the act as incommunicable. The same verb governs the making of man, three times in one verse for emphasis: So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them (Genesis 1:27). Image and sex are given in the same breath and by the same act, so that the two sexes are not a later social arrangement but the form in which the image was issued. The New Testament names the Agent: For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible… all things were created by him, and for him (Colossians 1:16). The Son is not the first creature but the Creator, and the thrones and dominions men fear are items on His inventory. And the same word describes the second creation: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works (Ephesians 2:10) — the new birth is a creative act, not a repair.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines CREATED as formed from nothing; caused to exist; produced; brought into being. Webster distinguishes the strict sense — to cause to exist without pre-existing materials, an act proper to God alone — from the looser sense of shaping or constituting from what already exists.

expand to see more

CREATED, pp. — Formed from nothing; caused to exist; brought into being by the divine power.

In the strict sense, to produce without the aid of pre-existing materials — an act of omnipotence proper to God alone.

In a secondary sense, to make, form, or shape out of existing materials; as, God created man of the dust of the ground.

Figuratively, to constitute or appoint; as, to create a peer; and in Scripture, to renew or regenerate the heart.

From Latin creo, creare — the root also of creature, creation, and recreate.

Key Scripture

Genesis 1:1 — "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth."

Genesis 1:27 — "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them."

Colossians 1:16 — "For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him:"

Ephesians 2:10 — "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them."

Modern Corruption

Theistic evolution reduces created to a word for a process God supervised rather than an act He performed, and the modern denial that sex is given in the creative act sets Genesis 1:27 aside at exactly the point where it is most explicit.

expand to see more

Theistic evolution keeps the word and empties it. If God created man by superintending a chain of descent from earlier creatures, then Adam is not the first man but a selected one, death precedes sin rather than entering by it, and Romans 5:12 loses the historical Adam on whom the whole argument of imputation depends. Genesis 1:1 uses bara of an absolute beginning and Genesis 1:27 uses it again of man; Exodus 20:11 grounds the fourth commandment in six days of making. The dictionary’s position is six literal days and a historical Adam formed from the dust, and it holds that the framework and day-age readings were adopted to accommodate a scientific consensus rather than derived from the text.

The second corruption is the modern separation of sex from the creative act. Genesis 1:27 issues the image and the sexed body together — male and female created he them — and the Lord Jesus grounded the whole doctrine of marriage on that verse: he which made them at the beginning made them male and female (Matthew 19:4). To say that a person’s sex was assigned at birth rather than given in creation is to treat the body as an accident laid over an autonomous inner self, which is not a new idea but the old Gnostic contempt for the flesh wearing therapeutic language. The imago Dei in every such person is affirmed without qualification; the claim that the body may be corrected to match the mind is named as a corruption of Genesis 1:27.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew bara (H1254), to create, with God alone as subject; asah (H6213), to make or fashion; yatsar (H3335), to form as a potter; Greek ktizo (G2936), to create, to found.

expand to see more

Hebrew bara (H1254) — to create; in the qal it never takes a human subject, marking the act as God’s alone (Genesis 1:1, 1:27; Isaiah 45:7).

Hebrew asah (H6213) — to make, do, fashion; used alongside bara of the six days (Genesis 1:31; Exodus 20:11).

Hebrew yatsar (H3335) — to form, as a potter shapes clay; the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground (Genesis 2:7).

Greek ktizo (G2936) — to create, to found; all things were created by him (Colossians 1:16).

Greek ktisis (G2937) — the creation, the thing created; if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature (2 Corinthians 5:17).

Usage

"In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth (Genesis 1:1) — creation out of nothing, by the word of God."

"Male and female created he them (Genesis 1:27) — the image and the sexed body given in one act."

"Created in Christ Jesus unto good works (Ephesians 2:10) — regeneration as a second creative act."
